title: Interfaith friendship
hookLine: A Common Word, a Muslim letter to Christian leaders on love of God and neighbor

cards: "Come to an agreement between us and you." That's a line from the Qur'an, and it became the title of a letter.
Not a treaty or a press release: a long, careful letter from Muslim scholars, addressed to Christian leaders by name, the Pope among them, along with the heads of churches East and West.
It doesn't ask anyone to change their faith. It asks them to look at two commandments both sides already say out loud.

teach.b: Start with the verse the title comes from, Surah Al 'Imran, in Pickthall: "Say: O People of the Scripture! Come to an agreement between us and you." People of the Scripture is the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians.
The Arabic for that agreement is kalimatin sawa', a word held in common, level between two parties. The letter asks: what word do we already share?

teach.h: LOVE OF GOD, LOVE OF NEIGHBOR.
teach.b: Its answer is two loves: love of God, and love of neighbor.
On the Christian side, it quotes Jesus from the Gospel of Mark, in the King James words: "thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart," and "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."

On the Muslim side it sets the Qur'an's call to love and remember God next to a hadith in Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase, that none of you truly believes until he loves for his neighbor what he loves for himself.
Notice what the letter doesn't do. It doesn't say the two faiths are the same, or ask anyone to agree on who Jesus is.
It says: here is ground we both already stand on, so let's meet there, and live in peace.

teach.h: THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: Some Muslims set another verse beside it, from Surah al-Hujurat: "We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Know one another.
Not merge, not argue anyone out of anything. Letters like this can sound lofty, but the word at the center of this one is the plainest there is: neighbor.

how: Muslims take part in interfaith dialogue through letters like A Common Word, mosque open days, shared meals and community service with churches and synagogues, and some point to 3:64 and 49:13 when they explain why.

o: meeting across faiths on shared ground, without merging them
blending two faiths into one shared set of beliefs
debating others until they come around to your faith

games.why: A Common Word builds on the two commandments, quoting the Gospel of Mark alongside the Qur'an and hadith, without claiming the faiths are the same.

practice: Bring to mind one person you know whose faith, or lack of one, differs from yours, a coworker, a neighbor, a classmate's parent, and see their face.

Ask yourself what you actually know about what matters to them, and find one honest, friendly question you could ask. If you pray, hold them in mind as a neighbor; if you don't, simply hold the question.
